Pod life cycle
Earlier in this book, we learned i d x _ 7 e 8 f 5 a f 3 that containers have a life cycle. A container is initialized, run, and ultimately
exited. When a container exits, it can do this gracefully with an exit code zero, or it can terminate with an error,
which is equivalent to a non-zero exit code.
Similarly, a Pod has a life cycle. Because a Pod can contain more than one container, this life cycle is slightly more
complicated than that of a single container. The life cycle of a Pod can be seen in the following diagram:
Figure 15.12 – The life cycle of Kubernetes Pods
When a Pod is i d x _ e f 2 e 3 5 5 5 created on a cluster node, it first enters the pending status. Once all the containers of the Pod are up
and running, the Pod enters the running status. The pod only enters this state if all its containers run successfully. If
the Pod is asked to terminate, it will request all its containers to terminate. If all containers terminate with exit code
zero, then the Pod enters the succeeded status. This is the happy path.
Now, let's look at some scenarios that lead to the Pod being in a failed state. There are three possible scenarios:
If, during the startup of the Pod, at least one container is not able to run and fails (that is, it exits with a
non-zero exit code), the Pod goes from the pending state into the failed state
If the Pod is in the running state and one of the containers suddenly crashes or exits with a non-zero exit
code, then the Pod transitions from the running state into the failed state
If the Pod is i d x _ 6 7 5 7 8 6 8 4 asked to terminate and, during the shutdown, at least one of the containers exits with a non-
zero exit code, then the Pod also enters the failed state
Now, let's look at the specifications for a Pod.

Chapter 15 492
In general, the declarative approach is strongly preferred in all established orchestrators, and Kubernetes is no
exception.
Thus, in this chapter, we will exclusively concentrate on the declarative approach. Manifests or specifications for a
Pod can be written using either the YAML or JSON formats. In this chapter, we will concentrate on YAML since it is
easier to read for us humans. Let's look at a sample specification. Here is the content of the pod.yaml file, which can
be found in the ch15 subfolder of our labs folder:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: web-pod
spec:
containers:
- name: web
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
Each specification in Kubernetes starts with the version information. Pods have been around for quite some time,
and thus, the API version is v1. The second line specifies the type of Kubernetes object or resource we want to
define. Obviously, in this case, we want to specify a Pod. Next follows a block containing metadata. At a bare
minimum, we need to give the Pod a name. Here, we call it web-pod. The next block that follows is the spec block,
which contains the specification of the pod. The most important part (and the only one in this simple sample) is a
list of all containers that are part of this Pod. We only have one container here, but multiple containers are possible.

Kubernetes ReplicaSet
A single Pod in an environment with high availability requirements is insufficient. What if the Pod crashes? What if
we need to update the application running inside the Pod, but cannot afford any service interruption? These
i d x _ 8 a 5 6 2 0 a e questions and more indicate that Pods alone are not enough, and we need a higher-level concept that can manage
multiple instances of the same Pod. In Kubernetes, the ReplicaSet is used to define and manage such a collection of
identical Pods that are running on different cluster nodes. Among other things, a ReplicaSet defines which
container images are used by the containers running inside a Pod and how many instances of the Pod will run in
the cluster. These properties and many others are called i d x _ 9 9 2 d c 9 9 2 the desired state.
The ReplicaSet is i d x _ 8 3 c c 7 8 5 9 responsible for reconciling the desired state at all times if the actual state ever deviates from it.
Here is a Kubernetes ReplicaSet:
Figure 15.15 – Kubernetes ReplicaSet
In the preceding diagram, we can see a ReplicaSet that governs a number of Pods. The Pods are called pod-api. The
ReplicaSet is responsible for making sure that, at any given time, there is always the desired number of Pods
running. If one of the Pods crashes for whatever reason, the ReplicaSet schedules a new Pod on a node with free
resources instead. If there are more Pods than the desired number, then the ReplicaSet kills superfluous Pods. With
this, we can say that the ReplicaSet guarantees a self-healing and scalable set of Pods. There is no limit to how
many Pods a ReplicaSet can hold.

Popular tools: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize
By now, you should have a good understanding of Kubernetes' core concepts—how it manages Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services to keep applications running in a desired state. In practice, however, managing all those
YAML manifests manually can quickly become tedious. As your application grows, you might end up maintaining
dozens or even hundreds of configuration files across multiple environments such as development, staging, and
production.
To handle this complexity, the Kubernetes ecosystem has produced a rich collection of complementary tools and
practices that make configuration management, packaging, and deployment easier, safer, and more reproducible.
Among them, three have become particularly popular: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize.
Let's take a brief look at each.
GitOps: Declarative delivery through version control
Kubernetes was built around the idea of declarative configuration—you describe the desired end state of your
system, and the platform ensures that this state is achieved and maintained. GitOps takes i d x _ 1 e 2 8 3 a 4 1 this principle one step
further by applying it to the entire operational life cycle of a cluster.
In a GitOps workflow, Git becomes the single source of truth for both your application code and your infrastructure
configuration. Every change to the cluster—whether it's a Deployment, a ConfigMap, or a network policy—is

that repository and reconcile any differences between what's declared in Git and what's actually running.

Kustomize: Native configuration customization
While Helm focuses on packaging and reusing application templates, Kustomize addresses i d x _ a 6 1 f 0 9 0 e a different challenge:
how to manage environment-specific differences without duplicating manifests. It allows you to customize
existing YAML files declaratively using overlays, patches, and variable substitutions, all without introducing a
separate templating language.
Kustomize works directly with plain Kubernetes YAML. You start with a base configuration (for example, your
application's Deployment and Service) and then define overlays for specific environments, such as staging or
production. Each overlay can modify only what differs—for instance, image tags, replica counts, or environment
variables—while the rest of the configuration is inherited from the base.
A simple example layout might look like this:
my-app/
├── base/
│ ├── deployment.yaml
│ ├── service.yaml
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── overlays/
├── staging/
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── production/
└── kustomization.yaml
To apply a particular overlay, you simply run the following:
$ kubectl apply -k overlays/staging/
Kustomize is i d x _ 8 6 5 a 8 9 f 5 now built directly into kubectl, which means you can use it without installing anything extra. This
makes it a lightweight yet powerful tool for managing variations across multiple environments while keeping your
i d x _ 7 1 a 5 5 b 2 e configuration DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).
Bringing it all together
In practice, these tools are often used together. Helm or Kustomize handle the packaging and customization of
Kubernetes resources, while GitOps provides the automation layer that keeps clusters continuously aligned with
what's defined in Git. Together, they transform Kubernetes from a manual deployment engine into a fully
automated, declarative delivery platform.
As you continue your journey with Kubernetes, you will see these tools and practices appear repeatedly—not just
in small projects, but also in large-scale enterprise environments. They represent the next evolutionary step in
managing infrastructure as code: repeatable, auditable, and fully automated.

523 Introducing Kubernetes
16
Deploying, Updating, and Securing
an Application with Kubernetes
In the previous chapter, we explored the fundamental building blocks of Kubernetes and learned how they work
together to define, run, and scale containerized workloads. We looked at the control plane and worker nodes,
studied Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, and Services, and gained a solid understanding of how Kubernetes
maintains the desired state of workloads.
Now, it's time to put all that knowledge into practice. In this chapter, we will deploy a complete, multi-service
application to a Kubernetes cluster, update it without interruption, and secure it using built-in Kubernetes
mechanisms. You will learn how Kubernetes enables continuous delivery through rolling updates, how it checks
and maintains the health of your workloads through liveness, readiness, and startup probes, and how to protect
sensitive information using Kubernetes Secrets.
Beyond functionality, we will also look at security best practices that every Kubernetes operator and developer
should follow—covering topics such as Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), network isolation, workload identity,
and secret management. Security is now an integral part of the deployment process rather than an afterthought,
and Kubernetes provides several mechanisms to help enforce it consistently.
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Deploy a multi-service application into a Kubernetes cluster
Define and use liveness, readiness, and startup probes to ensure high availability (HA)
Perform rolling and blue-green updates with zero downtime
Apply essential Kubernetes security best practices for production readiness
In short, you will learn how to deliver reliable, resilient, and secure applications on Kubernetes—skills that form
the foundation for running containerized workloads in the cloud, which we will explore in the next chapter.

Technical requirements
In this chapter, we will deploy and update a small multi-service application named TaskBoard on a local
Kubernetes cluster. To follow along, you need a working Docker environment and at least one local Kubernetes
option installed. The examples in this chapter have been tested on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
You can use any of the following local setups introduced in the previous chapter:
minikube: Recommended for this chapter. Provides a fully featured single-node cluster ideal for
experimentation.
Docker Desktop with Kubernetes: Convenient option if you already use Docker Desktop.

Quick Access idx_fa3852e6 can be used as a transition state toward a Zero Trust posture.
Organizations looking to replace their VPN can start by using Quick Access to rapidly secure all
private network traffic through Microsoft's global backbone with identity-based controls. Once
traffic patterns are understood and apps are discovered, they can transition to per-app access,
applying granular Zero Trust policies to each application, reducing lateral movement, and fully
eliminating traditional VPN dependencies.
